PRIVACY. A rule provisioned from a fallback scan detects only its own name as literal text, so 'Credit Card' stops detecting card numbers permanently - and the ON CONFLICT(name) upsert never replaces the row.
A fallback scan would reinstate the built-in regex over a pattern the user customised, silently undoing their edit.

replace: ON CONFLICT(name) DO UPDATE SET severity = excluded.severity, pattern = excluded.pattern;

Newly captured clips wait for the worker's idle poll instead of being embedded promptly, so semantic search cannot find anything recent.
Dropping the UpdatedClips half leaves an edited clip matched by the vector of its old text - semantic search answers with content the clip no longer has.
The in-memory cache then only grows on a full reload, so every clip captured since the last refresh is invisible to semantic search.
An async Task that throws faults its task, and since nobody awaits the detached append the failure vanishes. Search degrades with no record of why.
A second Start() leaks the first pair of subscriptions and pokes the worker twice per clip, and Dispose only unhooks the last pair.
Nothing outside the database learns a clip is gone, so the in-memory semantic cache keeps a deleted clip searchable for the rest of the session.
The sweep and both capacity caps delete silently and are the only routes the user never sees, so a cache told nothing about them never sheds those clips.
A subscriber would evict clips a rolled-back transaction leaves in place, so the cache would lose rows that still exist.
A no-op delete would tell subscribers to drop a clip that was never there, and a shared id space makes that a live eviction of the wrong entry.
The store announces the deletion but nothing acts on it, which is exactly the state this coordinator exists to prevent.
Compacting the vectors without rebuilding the slot map points each shifted id at another clip's vector - search then answers with the wrong clip rather than merely losing one.
find:
_slotById = slots;
            Volatile.Write(ref _cache, new CacheSnapshot(newIds, newVectors, survivors, dim));
replace: Volatile.Write(ref _cache, new CacheSnapshot(newIds, newVectors, survivors, dim));

find: Buffer.BlockCopy(existing.Vectors, i * dim * sizeof(float), newVectors, next * dim * sizeof(float), dim * sizeof(float));
replace: Buffer.BlockCopy(existing.Vectors, next * dim * sizeof(float), newVectors, next * dim * sizeof(float), dim * sizeof(float));

why: A service the view model constructor needs is left unregistered. This compiles cleanly and only fails when the container resolves it at launch, so nothing but a container test catches it.
A service is registered under a concrete type rather than the interface its consumers ask for, so the registration exists but does not satisfy anyone.

CF_HTML header values are UTF-8 byte offsets. Treating them as UTF-16 indexes silently truncates every clip containing non-ASCII text, and only a non-ASCII fixture catches it - an ASCII fixture is byte-identical either way.
find:
var start = ByteOffsetToCharIndex(html, startOffset.Value);
        var end = ByteOffsetToCharIndex(html, endOffset.Value);
replace:
var start = startOffset.Value <= html.Length ? startOffset : null;
        var end = endOffset.Value <= html.Length ? endOffset : null;

why: A surrogate pair is 2 chars but 4 UTF-8 bytes. Counting it as 2 desynchronises every later offset, which only an emoji fixture exposes.
Without the deadline a suppression armed for a write that raised no clipboard notification stays armed forever and silently swallows the user's next real copy.
The monitor coalesces rapid writes into one notification, so pending suppressions must drain as a batch. Decrementing leaves a residue that eats a genuine copy.
Ctrl+digit exists to save the user the Ctrl+V. Selecting and copying without driving the paste sequence is the old behaviour and looks identical in every view-model assertion.
Ignoring the range result makes Ctrl+9 on a 2-clip list paste whatever happened to be selected, which is a wrong clip pasted into the user's document.
Returning on the first non-blank pattern means only the top line of the exclusion list works; every app listed below it is still captured, silently.
Substring matching turns 'Code' into a pattern that also excludes every app whose name merely contains it, silently killing capture the user never asked to lose.
This is what FileSystemName.MatchesSimpleExpression does: it treats backslash as an escape, so a directory pattern like C:\Tools\* never matches a Windows path and the app is captured anyway.
An unanchored glob matches anywhere in the candidate, so 'KeePass?.exe' would also match a path that merely contains it - the same over-exclusion the substring mutant causes.
Dropping the parsed list on save leaves the user believing an app is excluded while every one of its copies is still captured.
Not loading the saved list back into the form shows an empty box, and the next save then wipes the exclusions the user had configured.
Record equality compares the list by reference, so without the structural comparison OnlyViewStateChanged can never see an exclusion-list change and system state is not re-applied.
A blank line is routine in a multi-line text box. Stopping the scan there silently disables every exclusion listed below it.
The setting saves and displays fine but decides nothing, so the user believes their password manager is excluded while every copy from it is still captured.
Loading and encoding the process icon on every clipboard change costs a shell round-trip before we even know the clip is wanted.
CurrentCount == 0 followed by Release is a check-then-act race; concurrent pokes both see 0 and the loser gets SemaphoreFullException.
A queued embedding request can poke a worker whose semaphore was already disposed during shutdown.
A child window whose Closing handler throws would abort the rest of MainWindow teardown and strand the remaining windows.
find: Trace.TraceWarning($"Failed to close the {name} window during teardown: {ex}");
replace:
Trace.TraceWarning($"Failed to close the {name} window during teardown: {ex}");
            throw;

why: Swallowing the close failure silently is the original empty-catch bug: the session log never learns which teardown step failed.
Building an OCR engine loads a language model; doing it per image made an import backlog reload the same model once per clip.
A blank request must fall back to AppSettings.OcrLanguages, otherwise the background queue silently OCRs in the wrong language.

var requested = string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(languages) ? _settingsService.Current.OcrLanguages : languages;
        var key = requested?.Trim() ?? string.Empty;
replace:
var requested = languages;
        var key = requested?.Trim() ?? string.Empty;

why: An untrimmed key makes ' en ' and 'en' different cache entries, so a padded settings value never hits the cache.
The cache exists solely to avoid reloading the language model; a lookup that never hits makes it dead weight.
Serving the cached engine regardless of key would OCR Hebrew clips with the English recognizer after one English clip warmed the cache.
find: if (_engine is not null && string.Equals(_key, key, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))

why: BCP-47 tags are case-insensitive, so 'en-US' and 'en-us' must not each pay for their own model load.

A miss means the language pack is absent; remembering it would keep OCR broken until restart even after the user installs the pack. The cache has no field that can hold a miss today, so this mutant adds the negative caching a future refactor might.
The fallback means the requested pack is not installed yet; caching it under that key keeps serving the wrong language after the user installs it.
StartBackgroundServices runs on a thread-pool thread, so a dispatcher-bound periodic timer never ticks and the coverage chip freezes at its startup reading for the whole backlog drain.
Falling through to the newest stored clip discards the clip the monitor actually reported, which is the whole point of waiting for it.
Treating the busy flag as always clear restores the old fixed-deadline race: a slow capture lands after the resolver has already picked the previous clip, so the hotkey marks the wrong one.
An off-by-one on the bound lets a wedged capture hold the hotkey past the limit the bound is supposed to guarantee.
Hiding the popup deliberately keeps the selection, so a hotkey that still reads it transforms a clip the user last touched hours ago instead of the one they just copied.

The model loads lazily and only the query path or the backlog worker loads it. Gating the query on it being already loaded means a fully-embedded history never loads it, so semantic search is dead from launch.
Reporting 'the model happens to be loaded' as availability makes callers skip the very query that would have loaded it.
QueryAsync runs per search, so failing to latch a genuinely missing model retries a failing load on every keystroke.
Enabling the feature runs a full embedding pass and then changes nothing, because the search bar has a second toggle that defaults off.
Opting in on every save, not just the off->on edge, silently undoes a user who unticked the search-bar checkbox.
Reading Current outside the write gate is the lost update: a writer queued behind another composes its record from what it saw before that writer published.
The debounced filter save composing a whole record from a snapshot reverts every setting saved since - the original lost-update bug.
Persisting the content display mode by rewriting the whole snapshot reverts any filter toggle saved since it was read.
replace:
var stale = _settingsService.Current;
            await _settingsService.UpdateAsync(_ => stale with { LastContentDisplayMode = mode });

why: The dialog snapshots the filter and view-mode state when it opens; writing that copy back reverts everything the user toggled while it was up.

Any batch containing a re-embedding is barred from the in-place append path, so it reallocates; growing 25% every time it reallocates is unbounded and reached the 2 GB array ceiling for a 1,579-clip history.
Growing to exactly what the batch needs reallocates and copies the whole cache once per batch, which is the quadratic backfill the headroom exists to avoid.

The header offsets are a claim about where the fragment is and real applications emit them a few bytes out; the StartFragment comments are the boundary itself. Consulting the offsets first truncates the clip or drags in surrounding markup.

Handing an unbounded string to a wrapping TextBlock costs minutes of shaping on the UI thread; a 600 KB single-word clip took over four minutes before the bound existed. Raising the cap keeps every symbol referenced so the mutant still compiles.

Avalonia line breaking is quadratic in the length of a run with no break opportunity - 80,000 chars took 3s where the same size as words took 97ms - so a copied base64 blob or minified script rendered as a document freezes the UI for minutes.
An Avalonia ListBox is not focusable, so focusing the list instead of its container silently does nothing and the dropdown becomes mouse-only.
find: return suggestions.ContainerFromIndex(index) is ListBoxItem item && item.Focus();

why: The window key handler tunnels, so without claiming Enter/Escape while the dropdown has focus, Escape clears the whole search box instead of closing the dropdown.

Down belongs to the clip list, which is the live result of the query. The dropdown opens whenever the query substring-matches a past search - most of the time - so sharing Down makes looking at the results unreachable exactly when the query resembles an old one.

The capacity readouts are derived from the settings draft. Extracting the limit properties to the child view model drops the notifications their setters used to raise, and nothing fails - the readout just stops updating.

The point of making sections objects is that the notification loop covers every section it finds. A loop reaching only some of them leaves the rest rendered against a stale filter - exactly the silent failure the old hand-written thirteen-line list produced.

An empty filter matches every section, so auto-expanding on it flings the whole form open and discards whatever the user had collapsed. The guard is the only thing preventing that, and clearing the search box is the common path.

Turning fuzzy matching off has to actually narrow the search to literal keyword hits. A fallback that runs regardless leaves the setting present in the form and inert, which no round trip through save and load would reveal.

The binding-error tests assert an empty collection, which is also what a listener that never receives anything produces. If the app builder stops routing binding failures to Trace they would all keep passing while watching nothing at all.

The Edit menu, the toolbar flyout and the clip context menu list the same transforms from two places that are kept in step by hand. A menu quietly missing an entry looks exactly like a menu that never had one.
Relabelling a transform in the code-built menus but not the hand-written context menu presents one feature under two names, which reads as two features to anyone who meets both.

A brush present under one theme variant and missing under the other resolves fine for whoever shares that variant and comes out unstyled for everyone else - so it is invisible to a developer running dark mode, which is all of them.

Saving writes two files that cannot be made atomic, and only one of them is destructive - a path change copies the database and deletes the source. Doing that half first means a failure to write settings.json leaves the library moved and every other setting silently reverted.

RaiseSelectionStateProperties is around seventy hand-written notifications. Dropping one is silent: the field keeps showing the previously selected clip's value until some unrelated refresh happens to raise it. This is the largest instance of a pattern that has already produced two real bugs in this codebase.

Checks the selection-notification test reaches more than one kind of property: the age chip is a brush chosen by bucket, so it only moves when two clips fall in different age bands. A test whose fixture cannot tell those apart guards the list in name only.

Setting SelectedClip moves the anchor, which is right for arrowing but wrong for a shift-click. Without restoring it, every range pivots on its own far end, so a selection can only grow - ctrl-click 3, shift-click 5, shift-click 1 gives 1..5 instead of 1..3 and there is no way back to a smaller range.

RecentSearches is ordered most-recent-first, so going further back in time means moving up the index while the key's delta is negative. Adding the delta directly walks the wrong way and hits a boundary on the second press, which made every entry except the two ends unreachable.

The SelectedClip setter coerces null back to Clips[0] while the list is non-empty. It reads as defensive noise, but roughly fifty SelectedClip? sites and the delete command's target resolution assume a selection exists whenever clips do.

GetCheckedOrSelectedClips narrows to the single selected clip when nothing is checked. Treating an empty check set as 'all clips' instead would silently make one Delete destroy the whole visible history.
replace: var checkedClips = Clips.Where(static clip => clip.IsChecked || true).ToArray();

why: A keyboard layout can report Key.None while PhysicalKey still identifies the position. Without the fallback every in-window search toggle stops responding on such a layout, and nothing logs - the user concludes the feature is broken rather than that their layout is.
replace: => key != Key.None || physicalKey != PhysicalKey.None ? key : physicalKey switch

why: Modifiers are compared for equality so Ctrl+Shift+R cannot fire the Ctrl+R toggle. Testing for a subset instead would let a broader gesture swallow whatever the user bound it to.

The suppression gate is one-shot. Arming it before the work that can fail - TryLoadImage returns null for any image over MaxClipSizeBytes - leaves the arm pending when the copy throws, and the next thing the user copies for real is silently missing from their history. The cost lands on the following copy, so it does not look related to the copy that failed.

The original ordering: arm once up front, then decode. A decode that fails leaves the arm pending and the user's next real copy is dropped from their history. Restoring it must fail the test, or the fix is not defended.

Ctrl+Down is what makes it safe for the plain keys to belong to the dropdown. Without it the clip list is unreachable by keyboard whenever the dropdown is open, which is the trap the old routing existed to avoid.
find: if (modifiers == KeyModifiers.Control && e.Key is Key.Down or Key.Up)

why: Review finding A18, second clause. CanAiTransform is true for any image clip because an image is AI-transformable in principle, but every text group inside the menu is gated on CanTransform, which is false for images. With no AI configured an image clip therefore offered a Transform menu containing nothing at all. HasTransformableTarget already accounts for both.

The trigram index stores 3-character shingles, so BuildFtsExpression drops shorter tokens. Choosing the FTS path because ANY token was long enough answers a different query from the one typed - 'go home' searches for 'home' alone and returns every clip containing it, which at the search box is indistinguishable from spaces meaning OR.

Hydration is the only thing that gives an image clip its bytes, and the preview is built before it finishes. Returning false unconditionally means the pane never rebuilds, so a selected image stays blank until something unrelated refreshes it. This is the risk taken by skipping the re-present for clips that did not hydrate.

An image clip's Content is the short text label stored beside the bytes. Copying that instead of the picture makes the global paste hotkeys paste a caption, and PasteAndDelete then destroys the only copy of the image.
The return value is what stops PasteAndDelete destroying a clip that never reached the clipboard. Reporting success when the bitmap could not be read restores the data-loss path.
Rich clips are 740 of this user's 1,638. Copying them as plain text loses every bit of formatting on a global paste hotkey.

Arming must precede the write to win the race against the change notification, so a throw leaves the arm pending. An arm that is never consumed is spent on whatever the user copies next, which then vanishes from history with nothing to explain it.

AvaloniaEdit virtualises per document line, so a single very long line defeats virtualisation and is laid out whole on the UI thread on every selection change - measured at ~18 us per character, linear across three doublings. Minified JSON, base64 and log lines all land here, and 852 of 1638 clips take this path.
The shortened stand-in is not the clip. Leaving it editable lets a save commit the truncation over the real content, turning a display guard into data loss.

The dropdown offers past searches, which matters most when the query matches nothing - and that is exactly when the clip list is empty. Putting the suggestion handling back below the empty-list bail-out makes Down dead in that case while Up keeps working, which is what made it easy to miss by hand.

SQLite's trigram tokenizer indexes Unicode code points. Measuring UTF-16 code units routes a two-character term containing a surrogate pair to the FTS path, where no matching trigram exists, so the search finds nothing even though a clip contains that exact text.
